speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: POSTPONEMENT OF MOTION TO EXTEND SITTING HOURS
speechtext:
Although I recognize that this is not strictly in order, perhaps I might say that after conferring with the Acting Prime Minister and one or two hon. gentlemen opposite, the government have come to the conclusion that we will not proceed tomorrow with the motion regarding sittings for Friday evening and Saturday. It appears that hon. members generally have not received enough notice and many of them have made a lot of other arrangements for the week end. I put the notice on yesterday, or I asked my hon. friend to put it on, just to protect the position, because if I had not put it on yesterday there would not have been the required 48 hours' notice. I told the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre at that time that I hoped to have some further conference before proceeding with it, but in fairness to the house I think we should not proceed with it this week. However, I hope it will be possible to proceed in this manner for the rest of the month and perhaps, after conferring with hon. gentlemen opposite, we might agree on one or two other changes in the sittings to expedite our work.

On the orders of the day:

What is the target date that the government now has in mind for the parliamentary summer recess to begin?

On clause 5-Temporary appointments. (Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I want to ask the hon. minister a question. Can he give us some idea of the salary of the experts who are going to be brought in by the minister?
Mr. Chairman, to reply briefly, "what they are worth".
Will the salaries vary between a minimum of $5,000 and a maximum of $15,000?
Mr. Chairman, no minimum nor maximum salary has been established. It depends entirely on the required services. Indeed, there are some experts who are very expensive and some less.

Mr. Chairman, can the minister tell us whether the experts whose services will be retained will be chosen by the minister, or whether they will have to submit to an examination comprising a series of questions or whether they will have to take part in a competition under the civil service commission?

Mr. Chairman, we shall, first of all, try to recruit those experts in the existing civil service, and it is only when the required talent cannot be found among federal employees that outsiders will be brought in.
Anyway, they may be appointed either by passing competitive examinations organized by the civil service commission, or by means of a contract submitted to the governor in council because of the limited time available. Briefly, if they cannot be found in the present civil service staff, their appointment will be made by a contract which will be submitted to the governor in council.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. minister just stated that they would only be

recruited elsewhere if and when the required qualifications are not found in the public service.
Yes, Mr. Chairman.
In this case, who is going to determine if qualified employees are to be found within the civil service or not?

Applications will be submitted to the civil service commission, Mr. Chairman.
(Text):

I should like to ask the minister a question. I have read in the newspapers recently that in the establishment of this department, branches will be set up across Canada in various municipalities. How many branches does the minister anticipate setting up at once and eventually, and what will be the total personnel of the department now and eventually?

The number of branches or regional offices as they are described cannot be determined theoretically in advance. We will have to discover as we go along how many are required. The areas in which they will be required will be determined somewhat by the program that may be evolved on behalf of the federal government to provide aid to manufacturing industry, and these regional offices should be located in relation to the regions in which they may be of the most help. Until such time as the department has been created, has analysed the problems and has proposed solutions and had them accepted it is difficult to say with any degree of precision exactly where they are going to work. I am afraid the same applies to the total number of people in these offices.
Does the minister have any idea what the total cost to the taxpayers will be for this department in order for it to function properly when it is eventually set up?

I have had no estimate made,
I regret to say, of the eventual cost. I do not think anyone could make one at this juncture.

Could the minister indicate whether it is anticipated that some of these people will be working for a dollar a year plus their pension premiums while still remaining on the payrolls of their companies?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I confess to astonishment at an earlier statement by the minister, who is piloting this bill through the house, that people from outside have to be called in to instruct the government and a competent civil service as to how to set up
1828	HOUSE OF
Establishment of Industry Department a department. He said these people would not be engaged in the long term development of policy but would be brought in in order to organize the department. We have 20 departments in the government service and the experience of generations in setting up departments, new ones having been formed from time to time. What in the world has happened now to make the government consider that they must bring in outsiders? I thought they had had their fingers burned sufficiently already with outsiders. Why must they bring in outsiders in order to do a job that the civil service is competent to do and has been doing over the years? This is a most astonishing development indeed.
The minister mentioned that they would be something like the dollar a year men that we had during wartime when most Canadians were serving for $1.30 a day. But this is not wartime. There is not the same tremendous rush to get something done because survival is at stake. Under wartime conditions it was understandable that additional help was required, but here we have this fantastic notion originating, I think, with the Minister of Finance, who is 20 years out of date when he relies on something in which he participated in 1939 or 1940 or around that time.
This is another example of the brushing aside of a competent civil service by suggesting that our civil service, with a score of trained and experienced deputy ministers as well as assistant deputy ministers, is not able to advise the government on how to set up a department, and that outsiders have to be called in because the government has no confidence in and does not trust the civil service. I think this again is a provision that has been carelessly drawn. The problem has not been thought out.
Clause 5 dealing with temporary appointments gives emphasis to what we have been saying about the bill generally, that it has been hastily conceived, badly drafted and is aimed at performing a function which is already being performed by the Department of Trade and Commerce. I was hoping that the Minister of Trade and Commerce would be here to stand up in the house and say those things that I suggested he would have to say with regard to the setting up of this new department, which cuts the heart out of his department. However, he is absent on other business.
I do point out, Mr. Chairman, that this is a ridiculous extra expense being placed upon the shoulders of the taxpayers of this country. It is going to add to the deficit of the Minister of Finance at a time when he is losing his revenue sources with each withdrawal of his propositions. This is an unnecessary additional expense because these


people are going to be brought in-we do not know how many-and they are going to be paid such salaries, upon such terms and conditions as the governor in council sees fit. This may mean expense allowances. They will be doing jobs for which trained people are already available within the civil service.

Perhaps I misled the hon. member who has just spoken in suggesting that these people were to be brought in for the purpose of organizing the department. What I should have said more properly was to assist in the work of the department during the organizational phase. I did, I think, place emphasis on the fact the people who would be brought in would provide the skills which are not now to be found within the civil service. An endeavour will be made by the civil service commission, and certainly by myself, to staff to the fullest extent possible right from the day this department is authorized with those men who are now in the public service of Canada, for which all of us have the highest regard. It will only be in the event that special or specialized talents are needed and cannot be found that outside people will be sought under the provisions of clause 5.

Do I understand the minister to say that the personnel will be taken on for organization purposes and, I assume, for certain staff purposes, and at a later time in the development of the department they will be blanketed into the civil service? Is that the intention of the minister?

I thought I explained that they were to assist in carrying out the work of the department during the organizational phase, and not longer than December, 1964. I am not too clear what the hon. member implied by his question, will they be blanketed into the civil service? This has a slightly sinister ring about it. These men will have to qualify for civil service employment like anybody else or they will terminate their relationships under this clause at the end of December, 1964.

May I ask a supplementary question. Then that would provide an opportunity to bring into the civil service all the party supporters of the Liberal party and, at a later time, blanket them into the civil service. Let us make no mistake about that. The minister cannot put one across and tell us this means anything different from what I have just indicated.
As the hon. member knows, one is not supposed to impugn the motives of any other hon. member. 1 think I would let the question die there.

I wonder if the minister could indicate to us what are the particular skills which the people who are to be brought in will possess and which are not possessed by the people in the Department of Trade and Commerce, defence production or other departments which are at present carrying on more or less the activities of this new department? I am wondering particularly if the minister could indicate to us how many people of this nature it is his intention to bring in for the organizational set-up of the department.

In response to the last part of the question, I am unable to say how many because there has not been, as yet, any attempt to recruit people or even to canvass within the civil service. Perhaps it would be inappropriate to do so before the department is authorized.
By way of example of the special skills, I think there are within government service at present a number of people who are intimately acquainted with the aircraft industry, with the shipbuilding industry and, within the Department of Defence Production, with the machine tool industry. There are not, in either the Department of Defence Production or in the present Department of Trade and Commerce, men with an intimate knowledge of and experience in the basic steel industry of Canada. If we can find such a man within the civil service he will be taken into this department. If not it may be necessary, during this initial period, to look to someone in that field to give us a start.

Has the minister any other examples he could give of the particular skills that will be looked for in addition to skill in the basic steel industry? I would think that perhaps the department of mines might have somebody with a considerable amount of knowledge in that area.

This would be a source to be canvassed, I agree. As I explained to the hon. member, this canvass has not yet been made. It would be premature for me to provide answers to questions which have not yet been looked at.

It would seem to me that if the government has no idea of the number of people to whom this section would apply, and has very little idea of the special skills that would be required, it is rather a questionable section to include in the bill.

I should like to ask the minister if he has any other technicians in mind in addition to the steel industry. I am thinking, for example, of the asbestos industry, which provides a great deal of revenue for
Establishment of Industry Department the country but which is concerned mainly with the basic material. There is not much finishing in Canada. Does the minister foresee any industries being established in that area?

I would sincerely hope that there could be developed in Canada intensive processing to a much greater degree than is the case at present, of the output of the asbestos mines themselves. This is a mineral which is partially unique to Canada and we should clearly go a lot farther than we do in the processing of it. This will be one of the functions of this department.

I was just interested, in connection with this new processing about which we are talking, in ascertaining whether the government intends to seek these experts within Canada, or are they going to be brought in from other countries to advise our people in the department of industry?
I think that in relation to Canadian industry we probably can find amongst Canadians in Canada the kind of help that is needed. It should not be necessary to go outside.

I should like to ask the minister a question in connection with clause 5, which says that no person appointed under subsection 1 shall continue his employment after December 31, 1964. Is it definitely decided that this department will be so set up that no advice will be needed after that date?

Specialized advice after that date will be needed. There is no doubt about it. To assume that this department will have all the knowledge and all the skills required is, as I mentioned earlier, presumptuous. The provision of specialized advice on an ad hoc, or even on a continuing, basis is provided for by clause 15, which we will come to later. Clause 5, which is under discussion now, deals with the temporary manning of the department until December 31, 1964.

The minister does not seem to be very certain what kind of personnel he is going to need in his department. My riding is a typical secondary manufacturing industrial riding. In fact the dominion government impinges on the affairs of manufacturers there in five areas, namely tariffs, taxes, export policy, the industrial development bank and shipbuilding. There are experts on shipbuilding in the Department of Defence Production, some of whom deal particularly with tariffs, which is the big worry of many people in my riding. There are lots of experts in both finance and national revenue, and on taxation
1830	HOUSE OF
Establishment of Industry Department there are experts in the same two departments. We have experts on export policy, and loan experts in the industrial development bank. What my manufacturers want are not more experts telling them what to do, but policies that will increase their businesses and give them a chance to survive.

Mr. Chairman, during my
absence I gather that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has been making some suggestions that I, as Minister of Trade and Commerce, was unsympathetic with the objectives of this legislation, and that I might be concerned about the weakening of my department. I would like to assure the hon. gentleman that during the time I was in private life I was one of the first private citizens to advocate the formation of a department of industry, and I did that with full knowledge of the responsibilities of the Department of Trade and Commerce of which I had been deputy minister at one time.
I believe it is essential for the period ahead that there be centralized, in the department of industry, the administration concerned with industrial development in Canada. I believe that this will add greatly to the efficiency of the government, and that it will leave the Minister of Trade and Commerce more time to devote to his primary functions, which are the promotion of trade.
May I add, Mr. Chairman, that the Department of Trade and Commerce became involved in industrial development because of its offices abroad. These offices were receiving inquiries about the possibility of establishing industrial plants in Canada. So, in order to service those inquiries, it became necessary to establish an office in the Department of Trade and Commerce to which they could be directed.
I believe we have gone far beyond this point in the needs of the country for industrial development, and I consider that now there ought to be a department primarily concerned with industrial development, rather than trying to divide the interests of the Minister of Trade and Commerce among industrial development, trade promotion and trade policy which are his primary functions.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Defence Production has previously informed the house that he has made no personal study, nor is he in a position to give any estimate on the cost of personnel in setting up this organization. This sounds bad; not only does it sound bad but it is bad. He is virtually asking this house to give him a blank cheque to hire people, without in turn giving the house any idea what the estimated costs will be. We have no target to shoot at and no facts on
[Mr. Smith.!

which to discuss this particular topic; therefore I think it should be deleted.

In the statement which he just made the minister used the word "centralized". We are afraid of that on this side of the house because the provinces do not like this word very much. I would like to know what the minister means by this word, because I think there is a danger of infringing on provincial rights.

I was of course talking about centralization of functions within the Canadian government. I was not talking about centralization within Canada. I was talking about the importance of efficiency within the Canadian government service, and that there ought to be located in one place all those functions relating to industrial development. I was not straying beyond this very limited meaning of the word.

I do not want to ask the minister to answer too many questions right away. I know the difficulties involved, and sometimes it is better to proceed and deal with them all at one time. However clause 5 says-
-the governor in council may appoint persons-
-and so on, while clause 15 says-
-the governor in council may appoint advisers-
-and so on. I presume any person who is an adviser is an advisory person, and it seems to us on this side of the house that there is a complete duplication except that clause 5 says "having special knowledge." Clause 15 permits the minister to appoint anyone even without special or general knowledge, and I suggest there is complete duplication between the two clauses. I am not asking the minister which should be deleted. I think he should have the general power under clause 15, and that he should be prepared to withdraw clause 5 which is clearly a duplication of it.

Further to the question asked by the hon. member for Macleod, I would like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who made reference to his experience in that department, whether he might have an idea how many and what type of personnel will be required?

If I can facilitate matters, perhaps the minister would be prepared to hold clause 5 in view of the questions which have been raised. We can hold that clause for a moment and then come back to it later when we reach clause 15.

I had hoped I made the distinction between clause 5 and clause 15. Clause 15 is a general continuing authority

for the appointment of advisers to the ministry and is really a standard feature in all bills. Clause 5, however, relates to temporary arrangements, in effect to provide for a lack of working personnel during the organizational phases of the department, and to enable the department to become effective at an earlier date than if we were to wait for the normal processes of recruitment and training by the civil service commission. It is a clause which sets out this purpose, and it is self determining. It will cease to have any force or effect after December 31, 1964, and the purpose of including it in here was to make it quite clear it was the intention of the government to proceed in this unusual fashion for a temporary, relatively short period.
I do not want to get ourselves dug in on this clause, which could easily happen and which would be somewhat unfortunate because there are other clauses which are much more important. We have raised this question with respect to clause 15, a clause which makes provision for appointments to be made by the governor in council in exactly the same way as clause 5 does. 1 was hoping we could proceed further with the bill and give consideration to these two clauses when we come to clause 15. Certainly, if we have a general power to appoint by order in council, as we have in clause 15, we do not need the powers in clause five. I do not know how many members will wish to discuss this point. There may be some. I was hoping to make progress. I made a suggestion. If the minister does not see fit to accept it, it may be that clause five will not go through and that it will be held up for some time. I do not know.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
I want to say one word on this. The minister was talking about these experts who would be brought in. I realize it may be difficult for him to say how many may be required, but presumably some estimate has been made. Is it 10, or 50, or 500? Can he give the committee a general idea?
I have in mind another matter. Would the minister be bringing in, for example, any expert or experts on the coal mining industry which is so important to both eastern and western Canada? If so, what will become of the dominion coal board? What would its functions be? Would it carry on in conjunction with these experts or would it eventually be eliminated? The coal board, to my mind, has done and is still doing a good job and I hate, frankly, especially in view of recent events, to think what might happen to the coal industry if the whiz kids really get hold of it.
4, 1963	1831
Establishment of Industry Department

I agree with the hon. member that the dominion coal board has been doing a first class job in relation to the coal industry in Canada. I can assure him it would not be the purpose of this department to endeavour to duplicate the functions of any other agency of the government or to arrogate to itself the functions which they are satisfactorily performing. If, for example, in relation to the coal mining industry any men were required, it would largely be for the purpose of affecting liaison between the coal board and the general apparatus of the department in relation to other industries-to make a bridge between the coal mining industry in Canada and possible coal consuming industries.

The minister has given us a statement telling us the purpose for which these people are to be employed. Has he considered that some of these advisers may prove to be of continuing value to the department and that the bill might have to be amended so as to allow such people to be retained automatically, in the civil service?
It seems to me that it is not desirable to have in the new department a conglomeration of people from other departments who had proved ineffective. It may be we shall need people from outside the country altogether. It is possible that countries such as West Germany, where remarkable industrial progress has lately been made, would agree to come here and participate in the development of industry in Canada. Subsequently it might prove that it was not to our advantage to let them go automatically because of the provisions which are at present in clause 2. I raise this question because it relates to one which I brought to the attention of our members the other night when I suggested that Dave Golden would be an excellent deputy minister. Someone has told me this was going to be a fact, and I would be curious to hear from the minister whether consideration has, indeed, been given to this suggestion.
Those who are chosen to join the staff of the new department will be valued more for the new ideas they are capable of bringing than, say, in terms of direct assistance to industry. A great many of our industries do not need assistance of a direct kind. The shipbuilding industry, for example, does not need people to give it advice. The companies are already in existence; they are extremely capable and all they need is an opportunity of producing. Their ability is proven. The aircraft industry, to mention another example, has already proven its capability. I think that is true of many other branches of industry. What are needed are new ideas. We are often surprised to read in
1832	HOUSE OF
Establishment of Industry Department newspapers and periodicals about industrial developments which are taking place in countries abroad, particularly in Europe. We read from time to time about new processes which, so far, have not been tried here.
As I have suggested, the people whom we should recruit are those who would be capable of throwing a new light on our industrial processes, and these people should have an opportunity to become permanent officials of the department. The minister would be well advised to bring in people from as wide a sphere as possible. There are many ways in which they could use their talents. For example, there is a terrific potential- for something-in northern Ontario. We have chewed up the rocks for years in the course of mining operations, but nobody seems to know quite what can be done with this residue, although some research has been done in connection with the possibility of making use of this material. Possibly, building brick, opaque plaques, or other useful material could be produced from it. People who can devise ways of developing these raw materials profitably are the ones who should be retained. If the provision now before us means that their services can continue to be used in the department, I am in favour of it. If not, I think the clause should be given further consideration.

I think the hon. gentleman has proposed two alternatives in relation to clause 5; either that we have no interest in affairs beyond December 1964, which is manifestly incorrect, or that after that date it would be expected that those who remain in the civil service would qualify under the civil service regulations. We will continue to have an interest in these people, and after that date people joining the department and remaining in the department should be prepared to and be able to qualify under civil service regulations. By that time they should be ready to qualify.

Mr. Chairman, I wanted to make one or two comments while the Minister of Trade and Commerce was still here because he made one or two rather interesting statements, one of them being that the thought it was desirable to set up a department of industry so that the Department of Trade and Commerce or the Minister of Trade and Commerce could have an undivided interest and could pursue the matter of developing trade. Doing a little rapid calculation, if I may call it that, I take it that the minister of this new department will be fairly busy and that there will be a rather profound division of interests. If the argument of the Minister of Trade and Commerce is valid for his department, I think it is even more valid in this


case. Because if I understand it correctly, the new minister will be in charge of regional industrial development. He is going to be in charge of industrial research; whether this includes the national research council or whether there is to be more specialized industrial research remains to be seen. Yesterday we had the announcement that he would also be in charge of emergency measures organization and assume all responsibility and functions previously handled by three different departments. He is also going to be the minister of automation, if I may call it that, because he will be charged with dealing with all the problems which arise because of automation. It does not necessarily spell out that this will also include the impact on the labour force, but we must certainly draw the inference from the provisions of the bill that he will be charged with the responsibility of automation as it applies to the industrial and perhaps the management side. In addition to that he is to be in charge of defence production and all that that involves.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the reason given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that he should not have his interests divided between trade and industry are even more valid in this case because, as I pointed out the other day, there seems to be a somewhat greater division of interest in all the things which are going to be assigned to the minister of this department than the two areas which seem to be so complementary to each other, namely trade and industry. I should like to have the minister reconcile this statement with what the government is actually doing in loading up the new minister with all these responsibilities. I will have something further to say on the next clause, because there is some question of jurisdiction which is to be included in this department. It seems to me a fairly complex situation.
While I am on my feet I should like to say a word or two about some of the provisions in the Glassco commission report which was discussed the other day. If the minister is going to do all the things which are apparently to be loaded upon him he will need more personnel, including personnel from almost all departments in the government today. I should like the minister to suggest whether the new minister can handle all these things without that division of interest which the Minister of Trade and Commerce indicates was undesirable.

Mr. Chairman, in the interests of making progress and trying to be of help to the minister, would he mind holding clause 5 for discussion with clause 15 and let us get on with other clauses in the bill? Would

he mind temporarily holding this clause until we can discuss clause 5 and clause 15 together? If he would agree to that we can get on with the work of the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I have tried to make the point that clause 5 and clause 15 cover two quite different situations. Clause 5 relates to the problem of rapid staffing with persons having special skill, who cannot be found within the civil service up to December 31, 1964. Clause 15 provides for the obtaining by the government of advice from outsiders, who are outsiders and will continue to be outsiders. They will not form part of the staff of the department nor be employees of the department. Clause 5 relates to individuals who would be temporary employees of the department rather than merely advisers. In this sense clause 5 is different from clause 15, and also for that reason is placed in a different position in the bill. It follows the principal disposition regarding staff, namely clause 4, the deputy minister provision. There is this distinction; and to ask the committee to postpone this clause until some later date merely means the resumption of the discussion, I would suggest, that we are now having without any greater degree of enlightenment.

Mr. Chairman, a short time ago the minister indicated the hope that many of these temporary employees might qualify for the civil service, following their one year's service. Would that qualification be based on their one year's service on a temporary basis or would they qualify in the normal way?
The normal way.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister, since he has given the committee the assurance that the intention is that the civil service will be used, why the words "civil service commission" do not appear in clause 5 or in clause 15?
Because the civil service and clause 15 do not come together at all.

My point is this. Who has a better knowledge than the civil service commission about the qualifications of persons presently employed in the civil service? In addition to that, who has a better knowledge of the qualifications of the people whom they are examining day after day and who, for one reason or another, may not qualify for the position being considered at the moment? Having that knowledge at the disposal of the civil service commission, it seems to me something which should be incorporated in the clause.

I mentioned just before the hon. gentleman came in that advice would be sought of the civil service commission as to the availability within the present government service of the kind of person being sought, and it would be in light of the inability of the civil service commission to furnish from within the public service of Canada at that moment the kind of person sought that recourse would be had to this clause. I do not think I will yield to anybody in my high regard for the present public service of Canada, and my strong view is that continuous recourse should be had to the public service before looking elsewhere. This is, in a sense, a residual clause. In the absence of the ability of the civil service commission to find, from within the government service, the kind of persons sought, then recourse would be had to this clause, but not for longer than the period mentioned.
Mr. Chairman, will the minister assure us that persons employed under clause 5 will not be paid at a higher rate of salary than persons within the civil service, for comparative jobs?

I do not think it is possible to give that assurance, Mr. Chairman. Obviously, if you are going to get a man away from his business for a period of four months, it is probable that you are going to have to pay him a monthly salary which is higher than one would expect to pay a man who was engaging in the same job as part of a life's career.
Then if he was a very valuable employee and you wanted to keep him on after December 31, 1964, you would have to ask him to take a reduction in pay to stay on in the civil service?
That is correct.

Mr. Chairman, listening to the answers the minister has been giving in regard to this clause I am becoming more and more convinced that the clause is something that is not required in this particular bill. It becomes evident with every additional answer given by the minister today that the purpose of these people is to help with the organizing of the department, and as far as I can see we have people qualified to undertake that work in the public service of Canada at the present time. If we compare this clause with clause 15, there is also in clause 15 the power to secure the services on a temporary basis of those who may advise the minister and the department with regard to any manufacturing industry in any part of this nation.
1834	HOUSE OF
Establishment of Industry Department

As the hon. member knows, Mr. Chairman, under the legislation setting up the wheat board there is provision both for employees of the wheat board itself and an advisory committee to the wheat board. To use this as an analogy, clause 5 relates to the staff of the department itself and clause 15 relates to the provision of advisers in the same sense as advisers to the wheat board or the advisory committee to the wheat board. The hon. member will agree that these two functions are quite different and the kind of man required is quite different.
The hon. member suggested that the purpose of clause 5 is to provide persons to organize the department. I do not think it would particularly need someone with an intimate knowledge of and experience in the basic steel industry to organize a government department. The purpose is not to provide advice on organization, but to provide advice in relation to the steel industry.

I realize, Mr. Chairman, the importance of the steel industry to a department such as this, but it would seem to me that you might need a man for longer than the temporary period indicated in this measure. Would not an adviser in that capacity be required on a more permanent basis than would be provided under clause 15?

Mr. Chairman, those who would be appointed under clause 15 would be advisers on a continuing basis. They would not be employees of the department; they would come from outside and would continue, in that sense, to remain outside. Their functions would be as advisers and they would not be on the staff of the department. However, under clause 5 provision is made for the appointment of individuals who in the initial business organizing phase of the department will constitute, where they cannot be found from within the civil service, the staff of that department. If those individuals who are appointed under clause 5 can be persuaded to and desire to remain on in those jobs, they must, prior to December 31 1964, qualify under the civil service regulations. Clause 5 deals with staff; clause 15 deals with outside advisers, or advisory boards or advisory committees.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to get some information from the minister. He is talking about civil service work and advisers. I was wondering whether he has considered the help that could come from another department, if people were employed for one year under the same clause. Also, in view of the fact that we are dealing with a specialized industry, we will need specialized technicians with regard to that industry. Will there be any foreign assistance, or perhaps


civil servants, coming in from other countries to help us with regard to the production in this specialized industry in Canada? I am not talking about mass immigration in this respect, but perhaps we will need to take in some other people to assist in this connection. Could the minister give us some information on this subject?

Mr. Chairman, in so far as people now in the public service but within other government departments are concerned, they are already employees of the government and no special clause is needed in relation to their employment. In so far as those outside the government are concerned, I have expressed the hope that we have within the present industrial structure of Canada sufficient talent and ingenuity to enable us to find the necessary staff for this department without having recourse to the United States, to the United Kingdom or to the European countries. It would be my hope, and indeed it is my belief, that we could find within the present industrial structure of Canada the talents that we need.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has given us an explanation as to the intention of dividing these two clauses 5 and 15. I have been reading them very carefully and I cannot see in the wording of the clauses themselves any difference in the authority which is granted. It seems to me, if I am not mistaken, that anyone who is appointed under clause 5 could just as easily be appointed under clause 15.
Or under the Defence Production Act.

Yes; or under another act. But clause 15 is the all-inclusive clause which, I submit, is wider than clause 5. Both clauses provide for the appointment of persons to advise and assist the minister, except that clause 5 uses the words, "advise and assist" and clause 15 uses the words "advise or aid". However, there is very little difference in effect, except that those appointed under clause 5 shall discontinue their service on December 31, 1964. To illustrate my point I would like to ask the minister this question. If a person who was appointed under clause 5 came to the end of his service on December 31, 1964, could he not be reappointed under clause 15 to continue his work in the same type of temporary appointment, and not be under the civil service regulations at all? It seems to me that in both cases they are governor in council appointments and are not subject to any of the limitations of the Civil Service Act as to examination or appointment. It seems to me that clause 15 is all inclusive,

that clause 5 is unnecessary and that anyone he would want to appoint could be appointed under clause 15.

Mr. Chairman, I think that the essential difference in clause 5, if one gets down to the words, is in the words "to advise and assist the minister in the work of the department". I am told that these words mean that this makes provision for such individuals forming part of the actual staff of the department and as such being able to do work of an executive character, to advise and assist the minister in the work of the department. In clause 15 the words used are "to advise or aid the minister". There is no reference there to "in the work of the department". The reason for the inclusion of those words in clause 5, was to make it clear that under clause 5 there was provision for the temporary engagement of people to staff the department.

I think that all of us have great regard for those people who may have special knowledge of the manufacturing industries. However, the minister has come to parliament and is asking us to pass this clause which will give the governor in council the opportunity to select people to bring in for the purpose of organizing the department. From what has been said here today this might be a qualification for some of these people to be taken on the permanent staff of the department after December 31, 1964, and in my opinion this clause should be deleted.

I should like to ask the minister whether he does not consider that a good deal of the specialized work which will devolve upon this new department is already being carried on by the Department of Trade and Commerce to quite an extent?
Yes.

I think it is even broader than that, Mr. Chairman. A lot of the functions that will be undertaken by the new department are already carried on in other departments. What efforts will be made to co-ordinate those functions and bring about some intradepartmental co-operation? This was a subject that came under consideration in the Glassco commission report, and I would imagine that some serious attention is being given to rationalization and co-ordination of the functions already being carried on in various government departments in this area.

As I tried to outline the other day, Mr. Chairman, the purpose of establishing this department is to try to bring about, to use a term which one member does not 28902-5-117J
Establishment of Industry Department like, the centralization within the federal government of all functions of government relating to the manufacturing industry in Canada. That is the purpose of the bill. It is recognized and has been stated that there are now being carried out in different areas of the federal government a large number of functions and duties which are here being devolved upon the minister and the purpose, as the hon. member has mentioned, is to co-ordinate the activities of the federal government in relation to the manufacturing industry.

This would involve the
transfer of some departmental branches to the new department of industry?
That is correct.

On the
question of centralization and the experts that are going to be brought in, may I ask the minister whether experts are going to be brought in from the corresponding departments in all the provincial governments of Canada that have to do with the particular functions that are going to be involved?
I am not sure whether the hon. member means that the department of industry is going to hire provincial government employees.

Are you
going to ask the provincial government departments corresponding to the Department of Trade and Commerce, for instance, to assist on a temporary basis?

There will be, of course, the closest collaboration between the new ministry, if we ever get it established, and all provincial departments of economics and industry; and one of my first acts would be to endeavour to get together with the provincial ministers who are concerned in this field. Clause 5, however, does not contemplate nor has it any relation to this point.
I understood the minister to indicate that the Department of Defence Production which he heads at the present time will be absorbed by the new department of industry.

Under this bill the Department of Defence Production will not be absorbed. There are a number of functions currently being performed by the Department of Defence Production which will be useful to the department of industry, but because there is only one minister they will not be duplicated within the department of industry. There will be the closest possible integration between the two departments. In the meantime, as I mentioned some time earlier, a review is
1836	HOUSE OF
Establishment of Industry Department being made of the functions of the Department of Defence Production with a view to the implementation of those aspects of the Glassco report which relate to expanding the functions of the present Department of Defence Production to cover areas other than merely defence procurement.

Mr. Chairman, we have been discussing clause 5 for some time. As some other members have mentioned, this clause could go together with clause 15 and it would save a lot of time. We have provision here for appointments on a temporary or probationary basis. At the end of 1964 they will not be eligible under clause 5 any more, but will come under clause 15. In subclause 2 of clause 5 it is specified that they will cease to be employed after the 31st of December, 1964 unless they have the necessary qualifications, but then they will come under clause 15. I think we are taking a lot of time on clause 5 and it would speed things up if we could hold it over until we reach clause 15.
I will repeat again to the hon. member-

Before the minister starts may I interject one request along exactly the same line. From reading clause 15 there would appear to be three words in it that are very likely to prove objectionable to the official opposition. Those words are "appoint advisers and". Would the minister be willing to let clause 5 stand until he has had time to consider whether he will withdraw the words that we find objectionable in clause 15?
I am not sure what are the objectionable words.

The words are "appoint advisers and". Those are the words that we find redundant and a duplication of words previously appearing in the bill. Without them clause 15 would then read: "The governor in council may establish advisory and other committees".

I might say to the minister that I suggested a while ago that I thought it would be helpful if he would agree, as we have very often done in the past, to allow clause 5 to stand until we come to clause 15. In the Defence Production Act almost exactly the same language, if not exactly the same, is used and there is provision there that the minister shall have all the powers. Like the minister I should like to see some progress made and I suggest that we allow clause 5 to stand, and go on with the other clauses until we come to clause 15. Then we can revert, or do as the minister sees fit at that time.
In the interest of progress-
And amity.
-and amity I would be glad to go along with this suggestion. I confess my inexperience in these matters.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: By consent shall clause 5 stand?

Agreed.
Clause 5 stands.
On clause 6-Duties, powers and functions of the minister.

I think the minister should make some statement in respect of this clause. I know there are various detailed questions that could be asked, and I know some of my colleagues here are worried about which, if any, of these powers are not now attributed to one department or the other. I say to the minister, in all seriousness, that perhaps he could resolve the doubts which exist in a good many minds in respect of the basic philosophy of this bill. Where does manufacturing or industry stop and where does trade and commerce start? Where is the line?
This clause sets out the duties, functions and powers of the minister, which extend to and include all matters relating to manufacturing industries in Canada. I suppose, technically, that is it:	all manufacturing.
Surely, the department must go farther than that. There has to be a relationship between this manufacturing and the selling or disposing of the products which are manufactured, as well as the interrelated question of tariffs. Frankly, without taking up the time of the committee, because that is one thing I do not want to do for various reasons, we get back to the question I asked the minister the other day: Where do we draw the line?
I assumed, from reading the newspapers, that the minister will head the new department of industry. Where is the line between this department of industry and the Department of Trade and Commerce? Where does one start and the other end? I think that is the general problem which is raised by this as well as another clause in the bill. I can assure the minister that I am not raising this question simply for the purpose of obstructing or delaying the bill. This is the last thing I want. I was hoping we would make further progress and that certain things could happen so that we would be dealing with something else tonight. Apparently we are not going to reach that halcyon stage between now and five o'clock.
I believe this is the fundamental question. There are other questions which certain of my friends have, but I should like the minister to try to clear up what I feel is the root

problem in the establishment of this new department, which would be imposed upon the present department. Where do you draw the dividing line between the functions exercised by this minister and the functions that are going to be exercised by the Minister of Trade and Commerce?

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member, in effect, is seeking a definition of manufacturing industries in Canada. It must be so because the duties, in so far as there are any duties incumbent upon this minister, are outlined in the bill. The powers, in so far as the minister has any powers, are outlined in this bill. The functions, in so far as there are functions, are also stipulated in this bill. We need merely to go on to subsequent clauses to discover what those powers are.
There is, perhaps, a question as to what is meant by "manufacturing industry". There is published by the dominion bureau of statistics a document known as catalogue No. 12501, occasional, and this is a classification of manufacturing industries in Canada. It is some 280 pages long. There are, in Canada, what are known as primary industries, and those are the ones relating mostly to Canadian raw materials in their initial form. We have now, within the federal government service, specific government departments relating to most of these primary industries, to wit, the Department of Agriculture in relation to primary food; the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys in relation to primary metalliferous products; the Department of Forestry in relation to forest products; the Department of Fisheries, the most important of all, in relation to our fisheries.
Beyond this stage of primary extractions, primary preparation, is the secondary stage of further processing. Popularly, this stage of manufacturing or industrial activity is called secondary, and it is with this phase of industry in Canada that the new department is concerned, secondary manufacturing in Canada. The classification or delineation of industries with which this new department will be concerned is contained in this large document. I would summarize to some extent by pointing out that there are 20 main classifications of manufacturing industries which I may read for the record:

The duties, powers and functions of the minister extend to and include all matters relating to manufacturing industries in Canada over which the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction.

Mr. Chairman, it seems that the matter raised at this time is a particularly delicate one, especially in eastern Canada. Could the minister tell us approximately where is the dividing line between the jurisdiction of the federal government and that of the provincial government, especially as far as the safeguard of provincial autonomy is concerned. I ask this question because all this seems confused and to constitute a certain infringement, because there is no dividing line, so to speak.

(Text):

When the Minister of Trade and Commerce was in the house he spoke of the functions that it will be possible to centralize in this department. I am rather surprised at his equanimity sitting here part of the afternoon and watching a major operation taking place on his department. Because of the careful consideration which it has been given in the past, I feel I should be very brief, but a few words with regard to the purposes of the company may be helpful in explaining the reasons for the introduction of the amending bill now before this house.
One of the principal purposes of the company was to widen the market in Canada for N.H.A. and conventional mortgages. To this end, the company was authorized to raise money by the issue of its own series A mortgage bonds and to invest the proceeds in N.H.A. mortgages, thus widening the market for such mortgages. The company was also authorized to raise money by the issue of series B mortgage bonds. The money so raised was to be kept separate from the money raised by the sale of the series A mortgage bonds and was to be invested in mortgages other than N.H.A. mortgages or, alternatively, in real estate for the production of income.
The purposes of the amending bill now before this house are threefold. The first is to provide for the use of a French name. This is provided for in clause one of the amending bill. The second purpose is to permit the company to invest funds in securities of, or guaranteed by, the government of Canada or the government of any province of Canada or any loans fully protected by such securities, pending the investment by the company of such moneys in N.H.A. mortgages. This is provided for by the new section 9A which is set out in clause 2 of the amending bill.
The third purpose is to remove any doubt that might have existed under the original incorporating statute that the company not only has the right to sell its series A mortgage bonds and series B mortgage bonds, but also has the right to pledge such bonds to any Canadian chartered bank as security for money borrowed, provided that the principal amount of the bonds so issued by way of pledge does not exceed the money borrowed on the security thereof. This is provided for in new section 9B contained in clause 2. New sections 9C, 9D, 9E contained in clause 2 of the amending bill are merely technical in nature and are made necessary by the provision permitting the company to pledge its bonds to chartered banks.
I should also point out to the house that this company is subject to the regulatory provisions set out in the Loan Companies Act. the second reading of Bill No. C-20, to amend the Annual Vacations Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a very simple bill, and very easy to understand. It does only one thing. Therefore my remarks will be brief and I hope the house will agree to the principle of the bill. The bill proposes an amendment to the Annual Vacations Act. As hon. members are aware, the Annual Vacations Act, which was passed in the 1957-58 session, provides that all employees who come under federal labour jurisdiction shall be entitled to an annual vacation. The main detail of that provision is that an employee who has worked at a job for two years or more gets two weeks vacation with pay. However, as the act now reads an employee who

has worked for less than two years but more than one year gets only one week's vacation.
At the time this legislation was presented to parliament we tried to get the government of the day to amend its own bill to make the provision for two weeks vacation with pay applicable after one year of employment. As a matter of fact, even before the government of that day brought in its bill I had introduced, in fact I had done so on several occasions, a bill calling for two weeks vacation after one year, and it was a matter of regret to me that the lead having been given and a better bill having been drafted the government of that day did not go all the way. The purpose of this amending bill is to correct that slight error. If this bill is passed it would amend the Annual Vacations Act to provide that employees coming under federal labour jurisdiction would in all cases get two weeks annual vacation with pay after employment for one year. There is, of course, provision as to what happens in the case of those who work for less than one year, namely that they get vacation pay on a pro rata basis; but that is a detail which we need not go into at this time.
I might say that when I introduced this measure in the days prior to the election of 1957 it did not get much support from the Liberals; but it did get support from the Liberals during the days when they were in opposition. Now they are back on the other side again, and I hope they do not keep changing back and forth. I hope that some of that change of heart, some of that contrition, some of that new approach that we have heard about, will express itself in the present government's attitude toward labour legislation. We have already had one instance of the Liberals talking out a piece of labour legislation which they supported when in opposition. I hope they are not going to do that today.
As I say, this is a simple bill carrying out a proposal supported by the Liberals when they were in opposition. It carries out one of the proposals advocated by them during the election campaign, namely an over-all labour code which would provide for statutory holidays with pay, for minimum wage legislation, for maximum hours legislation, and for two weeks annual vacation after one year's service. Because this is the position of the Liberal government, and has been the position since at least 1957, and because they took that position in the recent election campaign, I hope they will support this measure.
I wish to make it very clear, Mr. Speaker, that if this bill is given second reading I will not try to move it into committee of the whole and push it through all its stages in one day. If it gets second reading or approval
Annual Vacations Act
in principle it can, of course be dealt with at a later occasion. In that event I would move that the bill be referred to the standing committee on industrial relations.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, the principle of this bill is very simple. It is one that has not only had the support of the Liberals during certain times, but it had the support of the Tories in days gone by before they were in power. I hope we can correct all this musical chairs business that we have had in recent years and can get together today on something that at one time or another we have all agreed upon, namely that workers should have two weeks annual vacation with pay after one year's service. Therefore, I hope it will not take the house too long to reach a decision on this bill, and that the decision will be favourable.

My hope is as strong as the hon. member's that it will be in the very near future; and I feel quite confident that this will be the case. We in this party also recognize the need for a revision of our conciliation procedures and with the co-operation of trade unions and employers in this country we intend to speed up these procedures, which sometimes take quite a period of time, while at the same time not lessening the freedom of negotiation and not encouraging unnecessary conciliation when collective bargaining can effectively reach the desired end.
I mention these things, Mr. Speaker, to indicate that the subject raised in Bill No. C-20 namely revision of labour legislation, is only a part of the much larger proposal which we in this house must consider within a very short period of time. Based on the annual survey of working conditions of May 1, 1962 from the economics and research branch

of the Department of Labour, we see that 56 per cent of employees in industries under federal jurisdiction already get a minimum of two weeks vacation after one year's employment. This estimate excludes federal government employees who I believe already have vacation allowances at least equal to that proposed. It should also be pointed out that a large number of the employees in establishments not granting two weeks vacation after one year of employment do qualify for two weeks vacation after a longer term of service.
Some facts are clear, however, Mr. Speaker. The bulk of the impact of a reduction from two years to one year would be felt mainly by the railway industry, where provisions are for two weeks vacation after two years of employment. There are more than 130,000 employees in this industry, which is approximately 41 per cent of the total now under consideration. Twenty per cent of these already get two weeks vacation after one year's employment. Of the remainder it is difficult to estimate how many would be affected by the proposed change, as it can be expected that most of them would have more than two years seniority in their positions at this time. But regardless of the cost of the implementation of the principle embodied in this bill as affecting the railway industry, and indeed those other industries which do not have such a liberal provision at the present time-but I am speaking specifically of the railway industry-I think the workers have subsidized the railway by working for substandard fringe benefits long enough, and it is only proper that they should receive the same consideration as other citizens.
Consideration of labour legislation of this type is topical at the moment because the International Labour Organization recently completed its annual deliberations at Geneva, Switzerland. This organization, in its annual gatherings, with representatives of almost every trade union of nearly every country in the world, has over the years passed something like 120 conventions with the hope that all the principal countries would accept those conventions. Canada's record as regards accepting the conventions passed by the I.L.O. is very bad indeed; it is one of the worst of all countries. I think I am accurate when I say that less than 20 conventions passed by the I.L.O. have been adopted by Canada. We are sometimes told that this is because, first, Canada is a federal state and therefore, of course, the federal parliament does not have full jurisdiction in labour matters. But Germany is also a federal state and they have adopted a far greater number of conventions passed by the I.L.O. than has Canada. Another argument for the non-acceptance of

I.L.O. conventions in Canada has been that sometimes our existing legislation goes further. But I think, again, this is a fallacious argument, because it would be a very good example for Canada to set for other parts of the world if we were at least to adopt all the conventions passed by the I.L.O. as minimum standards, even if we do have better standards in this country.
I would urge personally that when the government is considering the adoption of the principle embodied in Bill No. C-20 it be included in a larger bill incorporating a number of measures such as were outlined in the Liberal platform in the past election. I would also suggest that in the latest convention passed last month at Geneva, Switzerland, by the I.L.O. there is a very worth-while subject which has not yet been touched upon, by federal legislation, at any rate, in Canada 'and which I think could very well be considered in the same bill as the question of increased vacation benefits. The convention comes close to a reform in labour legislation which I have long favoured.
I have long felt that there is a need for some sort of statutory grievance clause specifically applicable only to those employees in the country not covered by a collective agreement so that an employee who has gained what I would call a vested interest in his position by spending 15, 20 or 25 years at one job and who has built his home in the area and educated his children there because of the location of his employment, will not be lightly dismissed by his employer at the age of 55 or over merely because he has become half a step slower or because stampeding automation has made his skills outdated.

The Annual Vacations Act that we have in the federal field applies, of course, only to those employees under the jurisdiction of the federal government. In the last few days a situation has come to my attention which indicates that even the limited provisions we now have are not being applied to those to whom I consider they should be applied. I have reference to employees in the Northwest Territories. I have spoken to officials of a number of branches of the government about this matter and I would point out that the problem is not nearly as simple as it might seem to be when areas are involved that are not under provincial jurisdiction. However, I was interested to find out that in many cases there are loopholes in the present Annual Vacations Act which are taken advantage of by employers in the Northwest Territories carrying out contracts under the jurisdiction of the federal government. To make the act applicable in the Northwest Territories the government has to declare the project to be in the interests of the public of Canada. Sections 2 (a) (viii) and 2 (a) (ix) of the act read as follows:
2. In this act,
(a)	"federal works, undertakings or businesses" means ...
(viii)	such works or undertakings as, although wholly situate within a province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces; and
(ix)	any work, undertaking or business outside the exclusive legislative authority of the legislature of any province, and all other works, undertakings or businesses that are within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, but not including any works, undertakings or businesses of a local or private nature in the Yukon Territory or the Northwest Territories.
I know that occasionally in some of the provinces there are difficulties in applying some of the terms of what we consider to be the very minimum provisions of federal acts, and certainly the Annual Vacations Act falls within this category. Even if this amendment to the act were adopted it could be further amended to bring about the advantages already enjoyed in some of the provinces. This legislation is not always applied even though it is the minimum in some of the provinces and I would suggest that one Liberal premier has not seen fit to endorse the ideas of the previous speaker and has spent a great deal of time and effort, not in providing legislation to assist but rather to retard the advancement of a labour code and normal operation under reasonable and accepted labour legislation.
I believe that the way this act is worded, Mr. Speaker, would make it applicable to the employees of the contractor in the

Northwest Territories who want annual vacations with pay under the terms of this special statute. This privilege is being denied to them because there is a difference of opinion amongst the various departments such as the Department of Labour, Department of Public Works, Department of Justice and also citizenship and immigration, which have some administrative responsibility for these employees in the Northwest Territories.
I should like to suggest to the mover of this bill that a further amendment be included to make this statute applicable, along with a number of other statutes included in the federal labour code, to the Northwest Territories and the Yukon in all spheres in which legislative action has not been taken by the councils of these areas. The terms set by this legislation should not be considered as the maximum or even as superseding those provided by collective agreement, but should be regarded as minimal provisions for a labour code to be applied in those areas not covered by collective agreement. I suggest that the Northwest Territories, under the commission, have been sorely neglected in this field. I was shocked to find how limited the knowledge of the commission was in regard to what applied in the Northwest Territories and what did not.
I received a request from one of my constituents who is now working in that area to ascertain whether or not the annual vacations with pay legislation applied. I spent the greater part of three days talking to 50 or 75 people in the various departments concerned. About half of them were of the opinion this legislation applied and the other half were of the opinion it did not. It seems to me it is about time that we provided federal legislation in the areas not covered by provincial legislation. I hope that this measure will be referred to a committee and that the committee will give some consideration to an amendment to the annual vacations with pay act which will provide the employees in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon with this coverage. We had the case recently of a substantial uranium mining industry which today is facing exceptional problems of adjustments. This has nothing to do with tariffs; but still, here is a case where, were nothing done, there would indeed be a very violent dislocation of some substantial communities. It is this type of thing which was had in mind when the words "cope with exceptional problems of adjustments" were put into this clause.

Reference has been made to the uranium mining industry, which it is true has no relevance whatever to tariff adjustments, or to major tariff adjustments; but I would assume that the Minister of Finance, with his responsibilities for fiscal and financial measures, would have to have the overriding responsibility, in connection with any recommendations which were made, to deal with not one but perhaps, as the minister and all of us realize, many industries which will be confronted with very drastic problems in this period of adjustment. Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the minister could tell us whether there is any connection or relationship between clause 7(c) and clause 9 of part II.

Mr. Chairman, clause 7 generally relates to Canada as a whole and industry as a whole; it relates as much to healthy, prosperous industry as it does to what one might call ailing industry or ailing areas. Clause 7 encompasses the whole field, whereas part II, dealing with the area development agency, contains special provisions to meet the problems of areas of Canada, where, as a consequence of exceptional or chronic unemployment, special rather than general measures are necessary.

Mr. Chairman, I think the minister understands my position in regard to this whole matter, but since my advice was not accepted, and the government assumes responsibility for the measure, I will have to accept the position. With regard to clause 7, I would like to ask the minister whether he feels there is any conflict between the duties imposed on this department and the duties as outlined for the economic council. I see a great similarity here. I have read the Prime Minister's speech upon introducing the resolution and I will again refer to it. One of the points he makes as being the purpose of the department is to carry out the various ideas transmitted to it by the economic council. The duties of the council are to check into industry, into automation, into greater production, and so on.
I see a great conflict here, and for the life of me I still see added bureaucracy imposed on business. It seems to me we are trying to push a cart one way and we have taken the horse that was pulling it off the other end by some of the other things we are doing. I do not know what progress is going to be made. My information indicates that government has a large enough partnership in business now; and there seems to be a great deal of paperwork involved. I am wondering what is the conflict. Is the minister of industry going to be the minister to whom the economic council reports, for instance? If not, is the council going to report to another department? If so, we will have more running back and forth and more bureaucracy on the neck of business. the bill which is before us and with the conflict that I see in the two measures.

Mr. Chairman, because of the importance of this particular part of the department of industry bill I would like to make a few remarks in support of part II of the bill. This proposed enactment introduced by the Minister of Defence Production is in fulfilment of a commitment made by the Prime Minister of Canada in a debate in the House of Commons two years ago. At that time the Prime Minister, speaking as leader of the opposition, put forward the necessity of establishing an area development agency the purpose of which would be to provide a special thrust for development in areas of high and chronic unemployment.
This is the first occasion in Canada that legislative effect is given to a policy of dealing specifically with depressed areas. These areas may more beneficially be called designated areas or development areas, as they are in other countries. Canada is certainly not the first country; it is rather far down the list of countries which have taken action in this particular field. In the United Kingdom the most recent reflection of this policy was the enactment of the local employment bill; and there is no doubt about it, under that particular bill and former enactments the relevant department in the United Kingdom was able to attract industries and create jobs in areas which otherwise would have remained moribund. It is a matter of record that President Kennedy during his travels in the United States was appalled by the conditions of poverty and unemployment that prevailed in the coalfields of Pennsylvania, and apparently he vowed during those travels that one of the first things he would do if he became president of the United States would be to establish an area development agency the purpose of which would be to provide new jobs and new industries in these particular areas. I think it is a matter of record, Mr. Chairman, that even in the short time this program has been in effect approximately a billion dollars have been provided by the United States government for the development of new industries and new facilities in these particular areas.

I am sure that hon. members of the house realize we are not coping solely with an economic problem, the wastage of resources in the form of unemployed personnel; we are also dealing with a social problem and with the alleviation of harmful social effects that can arise from chronic unemployment. It is a fact that in certain parts of Canada unemployment has continued over a long period of time; that an abnormal percentage of the work force in these areas has remained unemployed. There is a stagnant pool of permanently unemployed in certain parts of Canada who, because of the lack of opportunity in these areas, ultimately lose their interest and capacity for work. Certainly it is a worthy objective to overcome unemployment for its economic effects, but also for its social benefits. Many of us in this house have been frustrated over the years at our incapacity to deal with certain communities in Canada that have been afflicted with special unemployment problems. Certain of these are well known to hon. members. They include Elliot Lake, Springhill and other communities in Canada. Here is an opportunity, under the area development agency, by which the government, the national authority can provide a special thrust for development.
We realize that coping with the problem of unemployment requires a balanced and manysided attack. The application of general fiscal and monetary policy, no matter how wisely developed and how skilfully executed may not have any effect in dealing with or curbing unemployment in these special areas. That is why there is a necessity for a special agency to provide special assistance for these areas of exceptional unemployment. If the measures contemplated in this particular enactment were applied generally, they would lose their effect in curbing unemployment in these areas of chronic difficulty. It is the intention to designate these areas through the development of suitable criteria. I understand that at the present time the Minister of Defence Production has set in motion studies by which these criteria will be developed. Surely part of the test of the designated area will be the level of unemployment, its duration over time and the rate of growth in the total employment in that area. After the criteria have been developed and the areas designated special assistance will then be made available to provide the special thrust required.
The proposal in the area development agency is a reflection of the policy of the government to give special support to designated areas or areas of slower growth. There is provision made in clause 10 of the bill by which new programs and new projects can be put into motion by the area development agency, a special agency within the 28902-5-118-j
Establishment of Industry Department federal government charged exclusively with this problem.
At the same time, in the elaboration of the municipal winter works incentive program the government has proposed that the federal share of payroll costs will be increased from 50 to 60 per cent in designated areas. Similarly, the government has undertaken to bring forward certain construction projects for which funds have not been provided in the current estimates. These are being brought forward to apply in designated areas of slower growth.
Hon. members will recall that in the budget the Minister of Finance provided major incentives for the creation of new industries in these designated areas. It should be pointed out that the tax incentives provided in the budget for new development in designated areas are the most ambitious fiscal attack ever made on this particular problem. These four instances I have mentioned provide very eloquent evidence of the wish of this government to deal with the giant problem of unemployment by tackling it in one of its most acute forms, namely, persistent chronic areas of unemployment. The Minister of Defence Production will provide a real service to Canada in applying his great talents to the prosecution of this new policy.
