It will be on that basis that we will attempt to achieve some of these developments to which the Minister of Labour made reference a few moments ago.

I have a question for the Minister of Labour in view of the highly political statement he made a while ago. In those depressed areas where people are relying on the building of houses for their livelihood, I wonder whether the Minister of Labour will recommend that as a special measure the 11 per cent tax on building materials be removed?

Mr. Chairman, I was seeking to catch your eye before the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis entered into the discussion and I have some trepidation in intervening now in a discussion initiated by two Nova Scotians, the hon. member for Digby-An-napolis-Kings and the Minister of Labour. I do not want to become involved in the airy clouds that apparently are floating between them.


I do wish to say that while I have no quarrel with any of the remarks made by the Minister of Labour, and while I appreciate the interest he has, coming from the part of Canada he does, in the topic he was discussing I should like to raise a point with the Minister of Defence Production similar to that raised earlier by the hon. member for Macleod. I feel that as this clause is now worded it may in effect be self-defeating. I think I can best make my point by reading the clause which is short, and is in these words:
The governor in council may designate as a designated area for the purposes of this act any district or locality in Canada that is determined to require special measures to permit economic development or industrial adjustment by reason of the exceptional nature or degree of unemployment in that area.
I certainly agree with the Minister of Labour that there are areas in this country where the chronic unemployment situation which he has described has prevailed. I am one of the members of this house who hope that is not going to be a permanent condition in Canada. For that reason I feel that the clause, as it is now worded, will in effect become a self-defeating measure. As I see it, once we have taken up the slack in this chronic unemployment that exists in certain areas, then if there is any real purpose in setting up this department we would hope the department would be free to continue to pursue a course of action which would ensure that, in the future, we would not again have areas of chronic unemployment.
It is for this reason I feel the hon. member for Macleod made his point well in drawing to the attention of the committee and the minister the idea that this clause should be so phrased that it would be possible for it to apply to areas where the exceptional nature or degree of unemployment may not exist. I do not believe anyone in this house would quarrel with the idea that areas in which chronic unemployment does exist should have top priority in respect of any application of this provision. However, if I understood some of the phrases correctly that were used by the Minister of Labour he was, himself, implying that while this measure was primarily directed towards these areas of chronic unemployment, it could embrace a broader sphere.
I feel this clause, as it is worded, very definitely and specifically limits activity to those areas designated. I should like to suggest to the minister that he consider rewording this clause so that while priority would be given to areas of exceptional unemployment, activity would not be limited to those areas. As I believe the hon. member for Macleod correctly pointed out, there may be certain

conditions in areas under which it may be desirable, not only from an economic point of view but also from a social point of view, to have the attention of the area council under this part of the act directed towards their development. There may not be at the moment any great numbers in that area either employed or unemployed, but there may be a natural opportunity to assure that the slack in the economy can be taken up. I would, in all seriousness, suggest that the minister give consideration to a modification of clause 9 so that, while it would make it clear that the immediate intent would be to deal with areas in which there is high unemployment, once that question had been dealt with the functioning of the department and of the area council set up in this area would not end.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word or two in furtherance of the argument that has been put forward by the hon. member for Macleod and the hon. member who has just taken his seat. We all know that one the great factors entering into the high cost economy that has developed in Canada has been transportation costs. We also know that the recommendations contained in the report of the MacPherson commission are not going to appreciably reduce these transportation costs. It has occurred to me, as it has occurred to other members, that the restriction of area development by reason of the exceptional nature or degree of unemployment in a particular area, is limiting the use that can be made of this particular part of the act. This limitation may work an undue hardship on the people of some other area of Canada. I should like to add my words to those of the other two members and ask the minister if he would consider amending this particular section along the lines indicated by the two preceding speakers.

Mr. Chairman, the province of Ontario, for some time, has been, to use a colloquial phrase, horsing around with area development. It all began with one of the greatest gambits in face-saving by Premier Frost when he decided to set up a number of development associations. These, on the face of it, were regional entities. Unfortunately, perhaps, they were subsidized by the provincial treasury and they were able to offer salaries of from $10,000 to $12,000 a year to men to set up little bureaus that somehow gave local chambers of commerce in various parts of Ontario and certain municipalities the feeling that at last they had an agency that was going to go into area development.

Well, the story of these economic development associations in Ontario has been one of gradual decline in enthusiasm. As a matter of fact, in various parts of Ontario there has been a falling away of the membership since part of the funds to support them come from such bodies as the associated chambers and municipalities. It was quite apparent, about three and a half or four years ago that the economic development association idea in Port Arthur or in Ontario had pretty well gone bust; it was not getting anywhere.
Again, Mr. Frost was the excellent politician. As I understand him he always was able, in the Mackenzie King tradition, to procrastinate slowly and well, and the provincial government of Ontario began to move to something a little bit more definitive. This found its spokesman and its great expression in Robert Macaulay. They call him Bright Bob and a lot of other nicknames. He has been booming around the province now for several years and he has, in a sense, shoved to one side the economic development association concept which was originally within the Ontario framework, and has created what are called economic regional councils. We have had one now for well over a year and it is called the northern Ontario regional council. Ostensibly these councils are designed to plan, to co-ordinate, to integrate, to direct research and generally carry out purposes not unlike those that are set out in this measure, particularly under this area development section.
My impression of these regional councils in Ontario is that they are just a time-saving device and a receptacle for tremendous criticism. The regional units in Ontario, in an economic sense, that are dissatisfied I believe would pile up in areas such as southern Ontario, northeastern Ontario, north central Ontario, northwestern Ontario and eastern Ontario. These economic regions are being palmed off again with what I would call a substitute for real action, in these cases with regional economic councils.
I can make this point best from the northern Ontario council which seems to be headed by a fellow who is an executive with the steel company in Sault Ste Marie. It has a lumberman from Port Arthur on it, a Conservative local politician from Fort William and somebody from the Timmins area, and these people get together on the odd occasion a couple of times a year and talk about the things they would like to have. I nearly fell over when I heard the first study they got under way had to do with ways of developing better air service into northern Ontario. This almost seems fruitless when you consider the number of air licensed
1862	HOUSE OF
Establishment of Industry Department carriers we have. The men who make up that council are decent people and fine citizens, but they are in no position to give very much time or energy to the area development agency. In addition, so far as northern Ontario is concerned this is far too big an area. It is not a natural economic unit.
I can illustrate this in a number of ways. The relationship between an area such as Sudbury and North Bay, or Timmins and Kirkland Lake to Kenora, Fort William and Port Arthur is quite distant, and this is what I am concerned about in this clause it gives us no hint as to what an area is going to be.
We had the ridiculous situation under the previous government, when the hon. member for Ontario was minister of labour and we were fiddling and fooling around to discover when an area would begin to qualify for certain kinds of assistance. As I remember, it was dependant on its unemployment index or the unemployment insurance statistics.
One of the things that is very apparent is that if we get area development councils, or area development boards that try to take in more than one natural economic unit, we will land in difficulty and trouble. Second, we have to work within the provincial boundaries.
I know the premier of Manitoba told me, about two months ago when I was interviewing him regarding the success of the Manitoba inquiry and the recommendations it made, that he was proud of it and he thought it was going to accomplish something; but it was very limited. The first limit on the economic development that could take place with the Manitoba agency was just the mere fact that it did not have the resource, the power or the framework which the premier said he really felt lay with the federal government.
The other point was in so far as the natural economic unit idea was concerned. In many ways Manitoba could be looked at as something distinct, if you looked northward running into its northern hinterland and its water and forest operations; but as a farm area many of its problems, in an economic sense, are co-ordinated and liaisoned, if you can put it that way, with the provinces to the west. Therefore he felt area development was never going to achieve what it could in Canada until we had a strong lead from the federal government. But here again it is hard to know geographically just how this area development thing can be nailed down and dove-tailed.
I know in our particular region we can see it with the operations of ARDA. At long last the provincial government in Ontario has begun to move on ARDA. They have a man, whose name I think is Herbert Crown, and his


job is to go around and work in various regions of the province to get ARDA projects under way, in co-operation with the federal authorities and with whatever local agencies can come in. Again it is a very long, slow and difficult process, and no one really seems to be sure where the initiative should come from in so far as a local region is concerned.
However, I could put this to the minister. He comes from a big metropolitan area, and coming from a big metropolitan area, whether you like it or not, this conditions your approach; just as coming from more distant areas such as the maritimes undoubtedly conditions your approach to the kind of organization you want to see. And one of the things I experienced in my own region is that it is almost impossible for an area that is distant from the biggest political centre of power, which in Ontario is Toronto and federally is Ottawa, to conceive and to take the initiative for grand designs for itself without a tremendous amount of leadership from either Toronto or Ottawa.
I feel this point I have is important for any consideration that should take place, not because I have it, but because I think it is an important point that an area development agency should not be a passive kind of agency such as has been created all too often under federal jurisdiction. That is obviously one of the troubles with ARDA. With the initiative being left to the province its success depends very much upon the regional and provincial leadership you get. When this is weak or insecure, and where you are unable to bridge the distance from the provincial capital to the areas where ARDA programs can do the most good, you do not get the creation of the kind of program that is necessary.
I noticed throughout this whole discussion, particularly since the bill was introduced, that our Conservative friends have been worried about its emphasis, as they see it, on planning, bureaucracy and that kind of thing. If anything, I am of the opinion that their fears are a little bit over-exaggerated from their own experience of creating statutes that fall into areas such as that-
I wonder if the hon. member would allow me-
-and drive the boards to become the bureaucratic menaces that they seem to suggest.
